reference_settings.note: Previously converged states for the identical physical model are reused only as numerical references, never as timing samples.

methodology: Timed cohorts use one pinned logical CPU and one BLAS thread on a shared CPU host. Different cohorts can use different pinned CPUs on that same host. All source variants, reused QuTiP and ordinary qutip.mesolve are measured on that same CPU in two mirrored cycles (four warmed samples per method). All 51 returned density matrices are materialized. Normalization is disabled. TC lowering, compilation and first execution are separate from steady runtime; QuTiP reused constructs MESolver once outside its timed runs. Only within-cohort ratios are reported. Cached high-accuracy states from the identical model are numerical references only, never timing denominators. Separate accuracy-only rows retain their own CPU affinities and contribute no timing comparisons. The final forward plot and table cover 3–9 qubits. To complete the dense curve and table, all five methods at 8–9 qubits were remeasured together in new complete cohorts. Older 8–10-qubit forward records are archived separately and are excluded from the updated plot, table and ratios. The new ten-qubit cohort was cancelled by the user before any solve sample completed and is excluded from performance comparisons. Prior high-accuracy 9/10-qubit, eight-qubit work–precision, gradient and supplementary Dopri8 evidence is unchanged. Only reused QuTiP appears in the figure; ordinary qutip.mesolve measurements remain in the complete raw cohorts. The shared machine and SMT siblings were busy; per-sample wall and process CPU times, ranges and per-cycle ratios are retained.

historical.methodology: Shared Xeon Platinum 8458P CPU. All forward timings and the 8-qubit work-precision curves use one pinned logical CPU and one BLAS thread per comparison cohort, with four warmed samples per method in two mirrored cycles. Only within-cohort ratios are compared. QuTiP MESolver is built once per worker; TC is compiled once per worker. Returned density matrices are materialized for both methods. No output normalization. The separate 10-qubit tight-accuracy check uses the same eight pinned logical CPUs and eight BLAS threads for both methods; its runtime is excluded from the performance comparisons. The 9-qubit tight-accuracy check uses one CPU/thread. A single-CPU attempt at the 10-qubit accuracy check was stopped before its first result and restarted on eight CPUs; none of the completed timed samples were changed.

qutip_wrapper_audit.comparison: ordinary qutip.mesolve versus reused MESolver saved trajectories; no extra solves

source_audit.ordinary: qutip.mesolve wraps each static collapse Qobj in QobjEvo and constructs a new MESolver for every call.
source_audit.reused: The worker constructs MESolver(QobjEvo(H), static_Qobj_jumps, options) once and repeatedly calls run with the same initial state and times.
source_audit.static_path: lindblad_dissipator(Qobj) returns Qobj, so sum(collapse dissipators) combines the static sparse operators before appending the sum to the Hamiltonian QobjEvo.
source_audit.wrapped_path: lindblad_dissipator(QobjEvo) returns a compressed QobjEvo for each channel. QobjEvo addition appends elements without compressing their combined constant parts. MESolver adds this sum to its Hamiltonian Liouvillian, and Solver.__init__ retains that QobjEvo without a final compress call.
source_audit.rhs_path: QobjEvo.matmul_data iterates over its elements and applies each element separately.
source_audit.interpretation: Read-only inspection of the installed Python and Cython sources identifies both per-call solver construction and a different constant-term grouping in the RHS. Their shares of the timing gap were not separately measured; the entire gap must not be labelled setup overhead.
source_audit.fair_baseline: Use the faster reused MESolver as the main comparison with the compiled TC solve. The ordinary qutip.mesolve curve reports its supported public workflow without modifications.
